newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Shooting erupts in Central Africa after march.
newsitem.headline: Shooting erupts in Central Africa after march.

text.p: Troops loyal to Central African Republic President Ange-Felix Patasse and mutinous soldiers exchanged fire on Monday after a march by thousands of civilians demanding the resignation of the president, witnesses said.

The shooting, about a kilometre from the centre of the capital, broke out after the march dispersed, the witnesses added. Some accused loyalists of firing in the direction of the march. One unconfirmed report said three marchers were wounded.
The march began in populous districts controlled by the mutineers.
The impoverished Central African nation is in the grip of its third army mutiny of the year but four African leaders sent by a Franco-African summit had negotiated a truce earlier this month.
French troops, stationed in Bangui and who intervened in May under a defence pact to keep Patasse in power, were not apparently drawn into Monday's incidents, witnesses said.
The mutinies, which began in April, were initially over pay but developed into demands, backed by the opposition, that Patasse step down. The latest revolt began in mid-November.
Patasse, elected 1993, has dismissed the demands as unconstitutional. The mutiny has turned into bloody feuding between his Baya tribe and Yakomas who dominate the ranks of rebel soldiers.
Mutineers control suburbs of the capital while loyalists and French troops control the centre.
The two sides on December 22 extended for one month a ceasefire and agreed to form a joint security commission.
The ceasefire was to stay in place until January 23, during which time rebels and loyalist troops would maintain positions.
"A joint security commission was established comprising 10 members -- five from the loayalist forces and five from the rebel forces," presidential spokesman Theophile Doumbe said at the time.
Both sides agreed to refrain from any acts or statements likely to compromise national unity during the truce period.

The accord was signed by Patasse, rebel leader Captain Anicet Saulet, mediator General Amadou Toumani Toure, the former military ruler of Mali, and French ambassador Jean-Marc Simon, who took part in the negotiations.
